64e957e7e30458f9.text: I'm Sona. Bats find their way with their ears, and that's what you'll learn here: to listen and know what you're hearing.

ebf47423d7f74a58.text: The drills use real multitrack recordings of "We Worship You", "Let's Have Church", "I'm So Glad I Met Jesus", and "God So Good". At the end, you'll mix them yourself.

ff9f7b454eb2924a.text: Sound travels through the console in order:

85eb19f0fdbab331.text: Mic , then Gain , then E Q , then Gate / Compressor , then Fader , then Main mix , then Speakers

b1006800d2b8948f.text: When something sounds wrong, walk the path in that order. Most problems show up early.

eda7e1c23fad989b.text: Gain sets how much signal comes in. Set it so the loudest moments peak in the yellow, never the red.

8fbf440e8f5e2513.text: The fader sets how loud that channel is in the mix. If your fader is way up and it's still quiet, check the gain.

2930a1dcbb69f1f1.text: The best sound is the sound nobody notices. We help people hear the words and worship without distraction.

5ca5859f1f17a5c2.text: That means anticipating, making small moves, and staying calm when something goes wrong.

26794a7ea3d6ee0a.text: A dynamic mic (like a Shure SM58 or SM57) is tough, needs no power and handles loud sources: vocals, drums, guitar amps.

4096cd0ffc965c5d.text: A condenser mic hears more detail and needs phantom power (plus 48V). Use it for overheads, acoustic instruments and choirs.

9e885b9ffe4d5a4b.text: Turn on plus 48V for condenser mics and active DI boxes. Dynamic mics don't need it. Old ribbon mics can be damaged by it, so leave it off for those.

2767f3b201506f53.text: Pull the fader down or mute the channel before you switch plus 48V, or you'll send a loud pop to the speakers.

507d7309361b0c84.text: On the M 32: the 48V button is in each channel's Config/Preamp section.

15fb20454e0de58e.text: Most stage mics are cardioid: they hear the front and reject the back. Point the front at what you want, and keep floor wedges behind the mic, where it hears the least.

6ab24282d319a7e2.text: Closer is better: more of the instrument, less of everything else, and less feedback.

eec48c62c5e78cc8.text: Kick: inside the port hole or near the beater for attack. Snare: an inch or two over the rim, aimed at the center of the head. Toms: the same idea.

4111f864742f98cb.text: Overheads: condensers above the kit, pointing down, to catch the cymbals and the whole picture. Hi-hat: pointed down at the hats, away from the snare.

b535bfe217039ba8.text: Guitar amp: a dynamic mic right on the grille. Aim at the center of the speaker for a brighter sound, toward the edge for a darker one.

d4cd52c4b6bdcfdb.text: Bass, keys, tracks and acoustic guitar usually go through a DI box. Stereo keys and tracks need two DIs: left and right.

54a12aa6b9cfacc8.text: A DI turns an instrument's signal into a balanced, mic-level signal that can travel down the snake without noise.

ea07ac0ee60d0ac1.text: An active DI needs plus 48V; a passive one doesn't. If you hear hum, try the DI's ground lift switch.

d72e2f342ef6e868.text: From the stage to your channel

2c9fe5f4e3e127cd.text: Each mic or DI plugs into a numbered input on the stage box. The snake carries it to the console, where it lands on a channel.

7ce536715984cfb5.text: The input list (in Planning Center) says what goes in each number. Plug in by the list, label everything, and line check every input before the band arrives.

c1450fa492c12879.text: XLR cables carry mics and DIs. Instrument (1/4-inch) cables go from an instrument to its amp or DI.

8c34a1450fb1e8b4.text: Wrap cables over-under so they lie flat and don't kink, and tape down anything people walk over.

ca9f6f492fe4feac.text: A microphone puts out a tiny signal. The preamp gain turns it up to a healthy working level, and everything after it (E Q, compression, plugins, faders, the recording) depends on it.

a989da403181dbd9.text: On the M 32: the Gain knob in each channel's preamp section, with the input meter right beside it.

8cdcda128fe6a224.text: Digital meters read in D B F S, where 0 means clipping. At soundcheck, aim for peaks around minus 18 to minus 6 D B F S: in the yellow, never red.

3c53b35a670c4a2c.text: That leaves headroom, a safety margin for the moment someone sings louder than they did at soundcheck.

279493066f52ea0f.text: Too low: you push the fader up and the hiss comes up with it. Too high: the preamp clips, and no fader, E Q or plugin can undo it.

17d003bfce093786.text: Set gain at soundcheck while each person plays or sings their loudest part. Then mix with the faders, keeping most of them near 0 D B (unity), where small moves are most precise.

71ed33e5d5315327.text: During the service, leave gain alone unless something is clipping. Changing it changes every monitor mix and the recording too.

fd39dda1e94d265a.text: Mic , then preamp gain , then channel E Q and dynamics , then plugins , then fader , then mix buses , then speakers and stream. Each stage should be healthy: never clipping, never starved.

5739886550793348.text: Analog-modeled plugins (like many Waves plugins) are calibrated for about minus 18 D B F S average, roughly 0 VU, so a healthy input level makes them behave as designed.

714e6079e67c19ac.text: On the M 32: Waves plugins usually sit on the channel inserts, after the preamp, so your gain sets their input level too.

715a664a7bb7dffc.text: Multitrack recordings usually come straight from the preamps, before the faders. So the gain sets the recording level, and fader moves don't change it.

31db62fd46eb8ed6.text: Record at 24-bit and let peaks land around minus 12 to minus 6 D B F S in Logic. Too low is noisy; clipped is permanent.

aaa8fe9a39c777ac.text: On the M 32: the card outputs feed Logic. Play Logic back into the board (switch the channels' input source to the card) for a "virtual soundcheck" on a weekday.

83fceb1fb4d9b8a9.text: We measure level in decibels. plus 6 D B is a clear jump. plus 3 D B is noticeable. 1 D B is about the smallest change most people can hear.

117ba68e8977502f.text: Try it: play the original, then the louder versions.

4a25eb7d11a53135.text: Live mixing is mostly small moves. If you can hear a 1 or 2 D B change, you can ride a vocal smoothly instead of jumping around.

a5e83979252e0d50.text: Our ears think louder sounds better. When you compare two settings, match their volume first, or you'll fool yourself.

e98cac68174580c6.text: A sound level meter reads in D B SPL. Every plus 3 D B doubles the sound energy, and about plus 10 D B sounds twice as loud to our ears.

26626e6cd00f1fc3.text: Your ears are a terrible meter, and they change over a service. Use a real meter at the mix position.

462612a6a32910d2.text: D B A and D B C

fcab105e733be99b.text: A-weighting (D B A) follows how our ears hear at normal levels, so it mostly ignores deep bass. C-weighting (D B C) includes the low end.

be8c2b0156f04d78.text: A bass-heavy mix can read fine in D B A but be overwhelming in D B C. Many churches watch both.

adca3a393066723a.text: Leq is the average over time (say, a 15-minute worship set). Peak is the loudest moment.

628395d83c017e25.text: Pick targets as a team and measure them the same way every week. For reference, Luke Hendrickson said Bethel's peak limits were 88 D B for the early service and 92 D B for the second.

7021fd93329a8be6.text: The NIOSH guideline: 85 D B A is safe for 8 hours, and every 3 D B louder cuts the time in half. 88 D B A: 4 hours. 91: 2 hours. 94: 1 hour. 97: 30 minutes. 100: 15 minutes.

972c9d476269046a.text: Rehearsal plus two services adds up. Wear good earplugs in rehearsal, and keep in-ear levels moderate.

08f11c111523794c.text: After loud exposure your ears go dull for a while (a temporary threshold shift), so you turn up to compensate and the mix creeps louder.

a91281eaa81abefd.text: Protect your ears before you mix, take short breaks, and trust the meter over your ears late in the day.

9d90dafde428a132.text: At lower volumes we hear less bass and treble, so the same mix sounds thinner when quiet and "better" when loud. Compare changes at the same level, and check your mix at the volume people will actually hear it.

708cb91ff3d72d2e.text: Streaming platforms measure loudness in loo-fs and turn loud streams down. YouTube plays back at about minus 14 loo-fs, so crushing the stream louder only costs you punch.

802a688da00f132b.text: Keep true peaks under about minus 1 dBTP. Logic's Loudness Meter shows loo-fs if you're checking a recording.

a4ffc3df89101b06.text: Look at the service in Planning Center: the order of service, who's singing and playing, and the input list.

2af65e5115515e80.text: Knowing the plan is half of mixing well. Surprises are what make Sunday stressful.

e0b9affb341130b6.text: Console and processing first; amps and powered speakers last. Off is the reverse: speakers first, console last.

835e55a5f4fc4288.text: That way the speakers never hear the pop of gear turning on or off.

1b235bcabc70137c.text: Before the band plays, check every input by itself: scratch or talk into each mic, play each DI, and make sure it lands on the right channel.

2beee569ae1eb765.text: Turn on plus 48V where it's needed and put fresh batteries in the wireless packs. A bad cable found now is easy; found during the first song, it's a scramble.

8ceb9c0224b7c1f9.text: Gain first, while each person plays or sings their loudest part. Then the monitor mixes, so the band can hear. Then a quick house balance.

bdb97621cb8204cf.text: If a wedge or mic starts to ring, ring it out now, not during the service.

920ee00d075ab5af.text: When soundcheck is done, save it as a scene. If someone bumps a knob or the console restarts, you can get it all back.

cc3e774fc709a8f3.text: On the M 32: open the Scenes screen and save to a new slot with a clear name, like the date.

7478ea7ec4135ea7.text: Right before the service: walk-in music down, the first mic up and ready, unused channels muted, recording and stream running.

c545c0bec1021166.text: Stay at the board and watch the stage and the run sheet. Make small moves, ahead of time: up before a solo, up before the pastor's first word.

2371e2ed5ac4c66f.text: If something goes wrong, stay calm and work it out from the simplest thing.

0f6f4e9a3ea2df1a.text: Stop the recording, mute everything, then power off: speakers first, console last.

fdab14d3bef86daf.text: Charge or swap batteries, put the mics away, and write down anything that broke or needs fixing for next week.

df34df888fe628e7.text: E Q turns certain frequencies up or down.

ab1e9fc9a825b681.text: Lows (20 to 250 hertz) are rumble and weight. Mids (250 hertz to 4 kilohertz) are body and words. Highs (4 to 16 kilohertz) are air and sizzle.

071922065b086871.text: Boom ≈ 100 hertz , Mud ≈ 250 hertz , Boxy ≈ 500 hertz

d0f4113dd5465e27.text: Honk ≈ 1 kilohertz , Harsh ≈ 3 kilohertz , Sizzle ≈ 8 kilohertz

08c024883b3dd639.text: Learn these and you can turn "it sounds muddy" into a knob.

eaefc2905bff423b.text: Fixing a problem usually means cutting the bad part, not boosting everything else.

a17d8ab9b381d0f3.text: Use a high-pass filter on every mic that doesn't need lows (vocals, pastor, acoustic guitar), usually around 80 to 120 hertz.

c7882cef25b32631.text: Every instrument has a usual place to start: where to high-pass, what to cut, and what (if anything) to boost.

f801b3a98a96e8a6.text: Can't tell where a problem is? Boost a narrow band, sweep slowly until the problem jumps out, then turn that boost into a cut.

2f6161a7709cbf37.text: E Q for the spoken word

437120a0f115eb6d.text: A speaking voice needs to be clear, not big. High-pass every speaking mic around 80 to 120 hertz, cut mud around 200 to 300 hertz if it sounds thick, and add only a touch around 2 to 4 kilohertz for clarity.

aa5c9857657aecdf.text: These are real voices from one of our Sundays: the pastor's sermon mic and the announcements mic.

16636006ba686b50.text: Handheld: held too close it gets boomy (proximity effect), with "p" pops and handling noise.

299cdfae4ae529c7.text: Headset: right at the mouth it gets harsh "S" sounds and breaths. Lapel: on the chest it sounds boxy and dull, picks up clothing rustle, and drops when the speaker turns their head.

33c0d824766ca2d1.text: Feedback is a loop: the mic hears the speakers and one frequency builds into a ring. Lapels ring most, because they sit farther from the mouth and need more gain.

29df4d1410ed3a24.text: Break the loop first: pull that fader down a little. Then fix the cause. Keep mics and people behind the main speakers, and away from floor wedges.

e26dede72593ea2f.text: Don't cut the ring on that person's channel: it changes their voice. If the same frequency rings on every mic, cut a few D B of it on the main L R E Q (or have the system tuned). From Church Audio Hot Takes with Nathan Fox and Jacob Lackey (The Worship Initiative).

e24a2feb63f487e3.text: When two mics hear the same source (kick in and out, snare top and bottom, bass DI and amp), their signals add together. If they disagree, they cancel, and you lose low end and punch.

a009c101a0774039.text: The polarity button (Ø) flips a signal upside down. If two mics are working against each other, flipping one can bring the whole low end back.

0759854ca933f017.text: In the live recordings in this app, flipping the kick-out mic adds about 4 D B of low end, and so does flipping the snare bottom. The bass DI and amp were already fine.

5a66ca7a1354cdeb.text: On the M 32: the Ø button in the channel's preamp/config section, near 48V.

15b8b67f09717819.text: Sound travels about a foot (34 cm) every millisecond. Two mics at different distances hear it at slightly different times, and the mix sounds hollow and phasey: comb filtering.

6d287784b288b500.text: Polarity can't fully fix a timing problem. Move the mics so they're the same distance away, or delay the closer one (many consoles have channel delay; Waves InPhase does it too).

6e377cf1d6c5f51f.text: Bring up both mics together, flip one, and keep whichever sounds fuller in the low end. Snare bottom mics almost always get flipped.

48523d8204cadf9e.text: Do it at soundcheck, and save it in the scene so it's right every week.

3e1196700fbc263d.text: A gate mutes a channel when it drops below a threshold, and opens when the sound is loud enough. Like me: I only pop up when something's loud enough.

0da6eeb2f2d7039c.text: This vocal channel has hiss and hum on it. Listen in the pause between lines.

5f6001159c257120.text: Set the threshold just above the noise you want gone. Too high, and I chop off soft words and the ends of notes.

446e18a14f4f051c.text: Toms, kick drums and noisy guitar amps. On a live stage, a tom mic hears the whole band; a gate keeps it quiet until the tom is hit.

599c0f1f0dcd04c2.text: Be careful on pastor and vocal mics. A gate that chops soft words is worse than a little noise.

24dac45714ac345e.text: A compressor turns down the loud moments so loud and soft parts sit closer together. Think of it as a hug that keeps things steady.

ea215fe05a298f6d.text: Listen to how even the words are.

bfc6482c60208d5f.text: Threshold is where the hug starts. Ratio is how tight it is.

46d2944c1e00aba7.text: 2:1 to 4:1 is gentle. 8:1 is firm. 20:1 is basically a limiter.

1c67ab77eeba3d6c.text: Attack is how fast I grab. Release is how fast I let go.

958cf7506b161828.text: Too tight and too fast, and the whole mix pumps and loses its life.

5f70db9d78ed836d.text: Compression makes things quieter, so we add makeup gain back. Compare at matched volume, so you hear the compression and not just "louder."

037f9b9847694878.text: A limiter is a compressor with a hard ceiling: nothing goes over. I build the dam so a dropped mic or a shout doesn't flood the speakers.

1bc1782de2f08983.text: When a signal goes past what the gear can handle, the tops get chopped off and it distorts. That crunch is clipping. Watch for red meters.

a4331299e827507d.text: Usually on the main outputs and the livestream feed. It's a safety net, not a volume knob.

58763efdc50303a6.text: If the limiter is working all the time, the mix is too hot. Turn it down.

2d10f8669bd5ca9a.text: Delay repeats the sound after a set time. Feedback sets how many repeats you hear.

e24fdfbf6c2741de.text: A slapback (80 to 120 milliseconds) is one quick repeat that thickens a voice. A long delay (a quarter or half note) is a clear echo.

67b8da65eff57bb1.text: Delays sound best timed to the song. A quarter note in milliseconds = 60,000 ÷ B P M.

e4c31428371bbcbe.text: "We Worship You" is 94 B P M, so a quarter note is 638 milliseconds. "Let's Have Church" is 170 B P M, so a quarter note is 353 milliseconds. "I'm So Glad I Met Jesus" is 180 B P M, so a quarter note is 333 milliseconds. "God So Good" is 77.5 B P M, so a quarter note is 774 milliseconds. Most consoles have a tap-tempo button for this.

81d03ec1e8b1ffaf.text: Delay on a spoken voice makes words hard to follow. Effects are for music.

84f9d138d36ef7b9.text: Reverb is the sound of a space: thousands of reflections fading away. It makes a dry vocal feel like it belongs in the room.

96a783c45e448c55.text: Small rooms fade fast (under 1 second). Halls ring for about 2 seconds. Cathedrals ring for 4 or more.

c22fc87d722dc436.text: A plate is dense and bright from the very first instant: smooth, with no sense of a real room. It's the classic way to make a vocal shine and sit forward.

5c7d92fddad52b39.text: A hall starts after a short gap, has distinct early echoes, builds slowly and rings long and dark: big and spacious, for pads and ambient moments. A room is short and natural.

488ed0a2eb64f8da.text: Vocals: a plate with 20 to 40 milliseconds of pre-delay is a common starting point, so the words speak first. Pads and ambient moments: a hall. Drums: a short room, or a plate on the snare.

9cc5e1cea3926d7c.text: Luke Hendrickson runs two reverbs on buses: one for the drums and one for the vocals. Two well-chosen reverbs beat ten.

c01a045bba31a652.text: Our sanctuary already adds its own reverb. Add a little to singers, and almost none to speaking.

d96a65c323bbfd65.text: If you can clearly hear the reverb, it's probably too much.

e329b299235438e8.text: A worship leader sings with reverb, then reads Scripture into the same mic. Pull the reverb down before they speak.

3cae6a4cd0dfabea.text: The smooth way: mute the send that feeds the reverb, not the reverb return. What's already ringing fades out naturally, even if you're a little late. From Church Audio Hot Takes with Nathan Fox and Jacob Lackey (The Worship Initiative).

83878e1a1eadda0a.text: Time effects (delay and reverb) and modulation effects (chorus, flanger, phaser, tremolo, rotary), plus drive.

f74ebfcf1290693d.text: Most modulation and drive live on the musicians' pedalboards and keyboards. At the console you'll mostly add reverb, delay and maybe a doubler. Knowing them all helps you talk with the band and spot problems.

ec61e3303484e6c6.text: Chorus layers slightly detuned, wobbling copies: shimmery. A doubler adds one copy a few milliseconds late, so it sounds like two takes: wider.

a11891f37738e977.text: A flanger is a very short sweeping delay with feedback: a jet-plane whoosh. A phaser sweeps notches through the sound: swirly and watery.

730d082e1cbeaa80.text: Both are mostly guitar and keys effects, used sparingly.

dd84d7ffff11797e.text: Tremolo pulses the volume. A rotary speaker (a Leslie) spins its horn, so the sound swirls side to side: the classic B3 organ sound.

ab642b6cc6747e8e.text: Overdrive adds grit and sustain to an electric guitar. On a vocal or the main mix, that same crunch means something is clipping.

8218fccce55772a7.text: Ping-pong bounces repeats left and right. Tape echo darkens and wobbles each repeat so it sits back. A digital delay repeats cleanly and brightly.

5d9d147986d434a6.text: Less is more: if people notice the effect, it's probably too much. Keep the pastor dry, and check with a musician before "fixing" their tone at the board.

0d8526aa680cd414.text: The room hears the speakers plus the band's own acoustic sound. The stream only hears your console, often on a phone.

22c7fc7bc2d2910f.text: Phone speakers can't reproduce bass. If the vocals aren't clear in the mids, people at home lose the words.

e241484b8e119523.text: Vocals and the pastor usually need to be louder on the stream than in the room.

23aa3d4ae85b59ba.text: Crowd mics belong in the stream mix (so it feels like church), not in the house speakers.

ea384f7997b5f980.text: Check the stream on a phone or cheap earbuds, and keep a limiter on the stream output.

65b698c1f7d1495b.text: The words carry the message, so the pastor or lead vocal always ends up on top.

ba149707a924b3be.text: You build a song's mix from the drums up (drums, bass, band), then set the vocal on top of it. The message is where you finish, not where you start.

9322135f2fa60449.text: Most mix problems are one thing too loud. Before you boost anything, ask what you can turn down.

a534c77e47cfc1cb.text: A warm hug, not a pinprick

d86d544546e7ea00.text: When it feels too loud, look for what's sticking out, usually harsh upper mids or a buried vocal under a loud band.

ab1b9a00c4221446.text: Don't cut the low end to make it quieter: the highs then feel brighter and harsher. A full, balanced mix with healthy low end feels less loud, even at the same number on the meter. From Church Audio Hot Takes with Nathan Fox and Jacob Lackey (The Worship Initiative).

dbab2e80330e39f7.text: In most rooms only the seats near the middle hear both speakers. Pan the electric hard left and one side of the room loses it.

45f0ed533a602ee2.text: Keep sole instruments (one acoustic, the keys, the vocals) near the center. A little panning, like toms, is fine. From Church Audio Hot Takes with Nathan Fox and Jacob Lackey (The Worship Initiative).

650e2242c039c329.text: A quiet prayer needs a different mix than a big chorus. Watch the stage, know the setlist, and move before the moment, not after.

f63a3215cd38d45f.text: In the last 30 seconds of every song, find who's up next, find their fader, and put your hand on it. From Church Audio Hot Takes with Nathan Fox and Jacob Lackey (The Worship Initiative).

20e3d16db902b3f4.text: The Nashville Number System names chords by where they sit in the key, not by letter. In the key of G, G is the 1, C is the 4 and D is the 5.

0b7973d27b6229dd.text: Change the key and the numbers stay the same. That's why bands use them, and why a sound tech who knows them can follow every call.

9afd54688adc6efe.text: In a major key: 1, 2-, 3-, 4, 5, 6-, 7°. A minus sign (or a small m) means minor.

92aaec949a49f7a9.text: Key of G: G = 1, Am = 2-, Bm = 3-, C = 4, D = 5, Em = 6-, F#° = 7°. Key of D: D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°.

ee3f2fa062edd0fc.text: Each number is usually one bar. Slash chords put the second number in the bass: 1/3 in G is G/B.

5899196b7db4b775.text: You'll also see things like ♭7 (a borrowed chord), a diamond (hit it and let it ring), and key changes written at the top of a section.

25ee18260fb670bf.text: Auto-Tune only works if you give it the right key. The setlist (in Planning Center) lists each song's key. Set the tuner before the song starts.

731c9558c1241756.text: Listen for the leader's calls. "Key up a whole step!" means your tuner key has to move with the band.

9401e3092c8d035f.text: Set the song's key, major scale, and a gentle retune speed. Luke Hendrickson says Bethel has tuned every vocal this way for years, and at a gentle speed it's transparent.

0fddead732e618a5.text: Too fast a retune snaps every note and sounds robotic.

cc26e6cfabc23bf2.text: Chromatic allows all 12 notes. It still smooths pitch, but never drags a note into the wrong one.

e101f34ceb1a20fb.text: Use it when a song steps outside the major scale (a 3 major chord, a ♭7, a minor 4), when you don't know the key yet, and in spontaneous worship that moves between keys.

aa41373da0322ada.text: Talking, prayer and scripture over a pad: speaking voices glide, and a tuner makes them warble. Bypass it. The pastor's mic should never have it.

2363f8e6d8d0000a.text: Also turn it off if it's audibly glitching on a singer, and for moments that are meant to be raw and free.

a487f424b3c74706.text: Before each song: set the key from the setlist (or recall the song's snapshot).

d99406d6f828a7bb.text: At a key change: move the key with the band. Not sure? Chromatic. Talking? Off.

724180b2f2ce80d9.text: Luke Hendrickson oversees audio mixing at Bethel Church. In a Churchfront masterclass he describes mixing as a language: learn the rules first, then you can break them.

145ca91492217f63.text: This unit follows his approach. It's one great style, not the only right way.

0051eefb89485a6a.text: Everything wants to live "downtown," roughly 100 to 600 hertz. A clear mix moves things out to the suburbs.

02e4f76505330556.text: Only kick and bass belong in the low end. High-pass chordal instruments around 200 to 400 hertz and vocals around 200 to 300 hertz (less for male voices).

57422c3cdfc72641.text: Drums, then bass, then acoustic and electric guitars, until it feels glued together.

aa3ab986ccce274b.text: Then solo the lead vocal and make it sound great on its own. Bring the band back in. The vocal should never compete with the band: the message has to be heard.

067132c0ca8a875d.text: When something doesn't feel right, newer engineers add a layer or another effect. Pros take something away and look for one compelling sound.

7c3ed5c938a8c68f.text: E Q first: a high-pass near 260 hertz, then cuts near 370 hertz, 900 hertz and 2 kilohertz, with just a touch of air at 14 kilohertz. He's a "subtractor."

d43b24c64720a6e4.text: Then gentle Auto-Tune, an LA-2A into an 1176 (only a few D B), a multiband compressor, a de-esser, and finally reverb and delay.

e3c3854be9f78d39.text: Luke runs everything in stereo, including effects. His vocal delay is an eighth note on one side and a dotted eighth on the other, plus a stereo slap (about 128 and 166 milliseconds).

b4bebb83b0d37ae6.text: Two reverbs (drums and vocals) and two delays (vocals), all on buses. Simple enough to run live.

24a1f0ae66c94094.text: Bethel's peak limits were 88 D B for the early service and 92 D B for the second. Big and clear at a moderate level comes from cutting the noise: stage volume near zero, a treated room, a focused PA.

a4df3eb26e7249b2.text: In the Sunday Mix, switch the style to Modern worship to be scored this way.

e5d76156c8fe35f8.text: Where should most of your input levels peak on the meter?

db1fe6b08a980b29.text: Healthy gain sits in the upper green or yellow with room to spare (headroom) for louder moments.

d058186ed3ef9a09.text: A channel's input meter keeps hitting red. What's happening?

cd2f567dfcc3f616.text: Red at the input means clipping (distortion). The fader comes after the problem, so it can't fix it. Lower the gain.

63c3453bcc05010a.text: What is an aux (monitor) send used for?

fc574fe790f1b87b.text: Aux sends let you build separate mixes, like what the singers hear in their wedges or in-ears.

ba995f9db8d79150.text: Condenser mics and active DIs need phantom power. Dynamic mics like an SM58 don't need it.

795852f6885e3e93.text: When should the band mix mostly be done?

869be4f788654725.text: Get the band mix done before the service so during it you can focus on who's leading and who's speaking next.

920e85c09b66c079.text: What does the gain (trim) knob set?

18538791cdfb7740.text: Gain sets the input level. The fader sets how loud it is in the mix. Gain first, faders second.

9264f2f660ad410b.text: Which order does sound travel through a channel?

c1cacc6c6bfe3783.text: Mic , then gain , then E Q , then gate/compressor , then fader , then main mix , then speakers. When something sounds wrong, walk the path in that order.

98f171eeb70742b1.text: People don't remember a great snare sound, but they notice a pastor's mic that isn't on. Know who's next and have your hand ready.

4f2924faf901f04c.text: A cardioid mic (like an SM58) rejects sound mostly from..

75bb3b49dc07726d.text: Cardioid mics hear best from the front and least from the back. That's why monitors go behind them.

72f16c521dcd86aa.text: A singer moves closer to the mic and sounds boomier. What is that?

c33fd71866cb705e.text: Proximity effect: directional mics add bass up close. A high-pass filter keeps it in check.

3d4a28a21ecf648e.text: Feedback is a loop: mic , then speaker , then back into the mic, louder each time, until it rings or squeals.

a01ae180a918be46.text: Pull it down first so it stops, then find the ringing frequency with E Q afterward.

b81e13e5c58e9432.text: Where should a lavalier mic be clipped?

00e49798d352f96b.text: Center chest, a hand-width below the chin, keeps the level even when the speaker turns their head.

d8ea023b8fd17d3d.text: In what order should you power on the system?

91207389849caeca.text: Speakers last on, first off. That avoids loud pops that can damage speakers.

f664a8a4952393c3.text: What's the difference between a line check and a sound check?

432cdca05b281634.text: Line check first (is each input alive?), then sound check (how should it sound?). Line check early so there's time to fix things.

87bc551f19677dd7.text: Where should the click track go?

dd930483292c4685.text: By the NIOSH guideline, about how long is it safe to listen at 94 D B A?

40f50a4e82406d2b.text: 85 D B A is safe for 8 hours, and every 3 D B louder cuts that in half, so 94 D B A is about 1 hour. Rehearsal plus two services adds up fast.

e45b98a54dd2069c.text: Per NIOSH, what happens to safe listening time for every 3 D B louder?

3ef10a02580ce714.text: 85 D B A is safe for 8 hours. 88 D B A: 4 hours. 91: 2 hours. 94: 1 hour, and so on.

c613d9d3cac830c1.text: By the NIOSH guideline, about how long is it safe to listen at 97 D B A?

024232d3c784310d.text: 85 D B A is safe for 8 hours, and every 3 D B louder cuts that in half, so 97 D B A is about 30 minutes. Rehearsal plus two services adds up fast.

9c6a4fca61d4e32b.text: Good isolation (a proper seal) lets people listen quieter. Encourage moderate levels.

0d69b181abf49add.text: Why might your mix creep louder through a long service?

2007219caf257981.text: Luke Hendrickson calls it temporary threshold shift. Trust the meter, take short breaks, and protect your ears before you mix.

e4dae4be56facf57.text: D B A rolls off the lows like our ears do at moderate levels. D B C includes the low end.

38005b80c63cf252.text: Every 3 D B doubles the energy. About plus 10 D B sounds roughly twice as loud.

aabc20eec923fc8a.text: Play each one as many times as you like.
